Not chosen: an owner setting for the prefix length (one more field nobody asked for, and the network already says it); PREF64 (needs raw router-advertisement sockets and privileges the core does not have); judging only the /96 reading (misses /48 /56 /64 carriers). Limits: a network without DNS64 learns nothing and keeps refusing some operator sub-prefixes, as before; the first judged address of a 10-minute window can wait up to 2 s for the lookup. | 2026-11-13 Known limit (Opus r2): a forged answer can still narrow the box-address check to the forged layout, so through a NAT64 translator that hairpins, a webhook/feed/SIEM URL could reach the box's own LAN address; the always-refused classes (loopback, link-local, metadata, multicast, unspecified, broadcast) are never narrowed, and the attacker must forge DNS on the box's LAN. Accepted: the box-address check cannot stay in every layout without bringing back the false positive this decision removes. |
| D-443 | **The syslog listener keeps its UDP and TCP sockets (and TLS on a box with a TLS configuration) open while the logs module is on, with or without sources; the sources decide only whose lines are kept (S-LOG-1, walk 4; replaces "no source, no socket" of WP-24 L2 and the per-source TLS socket of D-214).** (1) **Why**: walk 4 sent syslog from 192.168.18.145 before any source existed; core had no socket, so the datagrams met a closed port (podman publishes 514/udp+tcp on the host either way: `nc` to 514/tcp connects at the host and is then refused inside) and nothing was counted, so the D-421 hint ("<ip> sends syslog over UDP, but no source has this IP") could not appear, and the page said only "No device is sending logs to the box yet". The same held for a device sending TCP while only UDP sources existed. (2) **What**: `listen.Server.applyLocked` opens UDP and TCP always, TLS when `Config.TLS` is set; `SetSources` no longer opens or closes sockets, it only cuts the connections of a sender that is gone or no longer a source of their protocol (as before). An undeclared sender is counted in the existing 256-entry LRU (address from the socket, protocol, count, last time; never line text) and dropped: UDP datagram discarded, TCP closed right after Accept before any read, TLS closed before any handshake (D-214 (3)), so an open socket costs an undeclared sender nothing more than a TCP or TLS source already allowed. `GET /logs/unknown-senders` (D-421, 10 most recent, operator and up) then names it on the Sources page with **Add as source**. (3) **Unchanged**: module off = job cancelled = every socket closed (SYS-5, `TestNoSocketWhileTheModuleIsOff`); a bind failure is retried every 30 s and logged once per reason; nothing from an undeclared sender is stored (FORBID-5). (4) **The form says it** (walk 4 line 3): the protocol choice of the source form carries one sentence on what the box keeps ("The box listens on UDP and TCP and keeps this device's lines from either." for UDP; TCP and TLS per D-444). | Every leading syslog receiver listens on its port and filters senders after receiving, and says what it dropped: rsyslog `$AllowedSender` discards (and logs) messages of a disallowed sender at an `imudp`/`imtcp` listener that is up; Wazuh `remoted` listens on the `<remote>` port and logs "Message from '<ip>' not allowed" for an address outside `allowed-ips`; Splunk's network inputs listen on their port and `acceptFrom` refuses other hosts. A closed port cannot say anything, which is the walk 4 failure. Not chosen: open the sockets on the first source only (keeps the first device of a fresh box silent, the exact walk case); a "listen" switch on the page (an option nobody needs: turning the module on is the user's yes to receiving syslog). Sources: https://www.rsyslog.com/doc/configuration/global/options/rsconf1_allowedsender.html (as cited by D-421); https://documentation.wazuh.com/current/user-manual/reference/ossec-conf/remote.html (read: `allowed-ips` "List of IP addresses that are allowed to send syslog messages to the server", required for syslog); https://docs.splunk.com/Documentation/Splunk/9.1.2/Data/Monitornetworkports (acceptFrom per input; the inputs.conf spec page refused the automated fetch, behaviour taken from the docs index and Splunk Community answers); D-214, D-421 | 2026-11-13 |
| D-444 | **One device is one log source: the sender IP stays the key, and a UDP source also takes TCP from its IP; a TCP source takes no UDP, TLS only TLS (S-LOG-1, walk 4).** (1) **Why**: walk 4 could not declare a Mac that sends over UDP and TCP: a second source with the same IP is refused (409 `duplicate`) and a source has one protocol, so TCP lines from a UDP source were dropped. (2) **Options weighed**: (a) the pair IP + protocol as key (two rows for one device): needs a unique index change on `logs_sources`, a listener keyed by (IP, protocol), and splits one device's digest, baseline, state and line rate over two rows (signatures are grouped by source, D-30), which reads as two devices; (b) a set of protocols per source: changes `proto` in the API, the mock, the setup snippets (one protocol per device setup) and the table schema; (c) chosen, the smallest correct change: the IP stays unique, `proto` stays one value (the protocol the setup tells the device to use), and the listener's sender check is `listen.Accepts(declared, arrived)`: equal, or declared `udp` and arrived `tcp`. No migration, no API or schema change. (3) **Why that direction only**: TCP needs a handshake, so an off-path host cannot forge it as easily as a UDP datagram; letting a UDP source take TCP lets in nothing harder to forge than what it already takes. The other way would let a forged datagram pass as a device declared TCP to avoid exactly that, so a TCP source still drops UDP (and the D-421 hint names it: "<ip> sends syslog over UDP, but <name> is declared with TCP"). TLS stays strict both ways: its server certificate and optional client pin (D-214, D-435) are why it was chosen, and a plain line must not pass as it. (4) **Where it shows**: the source form's protocol hint (UDP: "The box listens on UDP and TCP and keeps this device's lines from either."; TCP: "The box listens on UDP and TCP but keeps only TCP from this device: UDP is easy to forge."; TLS: "The box keeps only TLS from this device, on port 6514."), and the 409 `duplicate` message ends "a UDP source also takes lines from its IP over TCP.". `UnknownSenders` (Go and mock) leaves out a sender its source now takes, with the same rule. An open TCP connection of a source edited from UDP to TCP (or back) stays; one edited to or from TLS is cut. (5) **Bound on the extra protocol** (review): a connection over a protocol the source was not declared with (TCP to a UDP source) counts against `Limits.MaxConnsIPOther` = 8 per sender, not only the 256 of `MaxConnsIP`, so a UDP-declared device (or whoever holds its address) cannot fill the 1,000 connections of the box and squeeze out the TCP and TLS sources; eight is plenty for a device whose declared transport is UDP. (6) **The hint names every protocol** (review): the unknown-sender table is keyed by address and protocol (256 entries), so `GET /logs/unknown-senders` returns one item per pair and the page shows one line per address naming all of them ("192.168.18.145 sends syslog over TCP and UDP, …"), instead of flipping with the last arrival; **Add as source** pre-fills UDP when UDP is among them (it then takes TCP too). Because a UDP sender address can be forged, the hint says so whenever a UDP sender is listed: "The sender address of a UDP datagram can be forged: check that the address is a device of yours before you add it." | The leading receivers allow one sender on several plain transports: Wazuh lists a device's IP in the `allowed-ips` of a UDP and of a TCP `<remote>` block (one protocol per syslog block), Splunk puts it in the `acceptFrom` of both its `udp://` and `tcp://` inputs, and the device is still one host in their search. Vedette has one row per device (the digest, the state and the inventory link are per source), so the same permission is expressed on that row instead of as a second one. Not chosen: (a) and (b) above. Sources: https://documentation.wazuh.com/current/user-manual/reference/ossec-conf/remote.html (read: protocol "udp, tcp"; for syslog one protocol per block; `allowed-ips` per block); https://docs.splunk.com/Documentation/Splunk/9.1.2/Data/Monitornetworkports (acceptFrom per input; spec page not fetched, see D-443); D-214, D-421, D-435 | 2026-11-13 |
| D-445 | **The dialog's connection test is kept for the profile saved with it, and the knowledge documents an answer carried are named in its sources (S-AI-1, S-AI-5, S-AI-7; walk 4).** (1) Changes D-424 (1) and (2): a Test in the Add or Edit profile dialog of settings not saved yet is kept in memory by the box, per admin (the last one only), with the connection it reached (provider type, API style, address, model, place and key; the key in memory only, as the profile snapshot already holds it), and only once the test's activity and audit rows are written. When the same admin adds a profile, or saves an edit that changes the connection, with exactly those settings within 15 minutes, that test becomes the profile's last test, success or failure, saved in `profile_tests` as before. Every save by that admin ends the kept test, so one test serves one save; an expired one is dropped with its key. Only the box records a test it ran itself: the add/edit request carries no test (an extra field is refused with 400 at the boundary), no test id and no claim. Other settings, another admin, a test older than 15 minutes or a restart give "Not tested yet". The place (internal or cloud) is part of the connection: it decides the proxy and the addresses the client may reach, so a test from one place says nothing about the other, and editing the place of a saved profile now clears its last test too (D-424 kept it). (2) When pieces of knowledge documents go with a call, the call's result carries the file names of those documents (each once, in the order sent; the names the box stored, checked by `checkDocName`), each in double quotes so a name with a comma still reads as one: Ask your data puts `Documents: "runbook.md", "vpn.pdf"` first among its sources, Explain adds the same line, and the evidence of a memory suggestion made from that question ends `; documents: "runbook.md"` (the walk 3 wording, with "tools read"). A call that carried no document shows no such line. The names reach everyone who can see the answer (Ask history, Explain, the memory card) and stay after the document is deleted: the answer's content, drawn from those documents, already reached those users, so the name tells them nothing more, and a source that disappears with the document would hide what the answer was built from. The document's text never appears. | (1) GitHub records the `ping` it sends when a webhook is created as the hook's first delivery, so a new hook is never shown as untested after a check that just ran (https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/testing-and-troubleshooting-webhooks/testing-webhooks); Home Assistant config flows validate the connection in the dialog and create the entry from that validated input (https://developers.home-assistant.io/docs/config_entries_config_flow_handler). Not chosen: the client sending the test result or a test id with the add (a claim the box would have to trust or look up anyway; holding the result on the box needs no new API field); keeping only passing tests (a failed dialog test followed by Add is honest as "failed", and "Not tested yet" would hide it). (2) RAG assistants name the files an answer used, for example Open WebUI's citations of the knowledge documents (https://docs.openwebui.com/features/rag) and Microsoft Copilot Studio's references to knowledge sources (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/nlu-boost-conversations); a passage that reached the provider without being named in Sources would be a hidden input. | 2026-11-13 |
| D-446 | **One rule for the box's own addresses in every destination an admin types (AI profile, custom feed and mirror, webhook, SMTP server, SIEM): Vedette never connects to itself, and may connect to another program on the machine it runs on (feeds, notify, logs, ai; S-FEED-4, S-NOT-1, S-LOG-3, S-AI-1; walk 4; replaces D-420 (7) and the "address of the box" part of D-86 (2) and D-208 (1)).** (1) **Before**: four rules for one machine. An AI profile at `http://192.168.18.141:18080/v1` (the appliance's own LAN address) was accepted and used, and so were `localhost` and 127.0.0.1 (in the core container that is Vedette itself); a custom feed at the same address was refused ("serve the feed from another machine"), and so were a webhook and an SMTP server; the container's gateway was refused by feeds and allowed by notify, logs and ai; logs knew only what vedette-host reports, not the container's own addresses. The SMTP sentence told the appliance user to enter the very LAN address it had just refused. (2) **Vedette itself, refused on every port**: loopback (127.0.0.0/8, ::1, `localhost`, `*.localhost`) the addresses of core's own container (its interfaces, read at every check) and the honeypot's decoy addresses (read from the honeypot's record at every check; a webhook to a trap would loop: incident, webhook, trap hit). In the shipped container that is core: its API, the sensor link, MCP on the container's address (D-395), the syslog listener; a request from loopback also skips the public rate limit (`core/server/publimit.go`). **The machine's addresses** (what vedette-host reports for the appliance; on every install the container's default gateway, the IP literals of `-hosts`/`VEDETTE_HOSTS`, `VEDETTE_BIND_IP` — the container-only compose passes it to core as an environment variable, which an older image ignores — and what `host.docker.internal` and `host.containers.internal` resolve to; without these a container-only install would reach its own API at `https://<LAN IP>:8443` through the published port) are refused **only on Vedette's own ports** — 8443 (interface), 8444 (sensor link), 8765 (MCP), 514 (syslog) and 6514 (syslog over TLS), the ports `install.sh` preflight reserves and the core Quadlet unit and the container-only compose publish — so no destination reaches Vedette through the machine's address and no SIEM forward loops back into Vedette's own syslog listener. Any other port of the machine is a normal destination: an Ollama, a mail relay, a feed server or a webhook receiver that the admin runs next to Vedette. The link-local, cloud metadata, multicast, unspecified, broadcast and NAT64/6to4/IPv4-compatible refusals do not change (D-442). Names are still judged on the resolved address at connect time (DNS rebinding), redirects still go through the same dialer. (3) **Unknown machine addresses** (vedette-host has not answered since start): feeds (only global unicast, D-208 (2)), webhooks (#157) and the SIEM socket keep their fail-closed rule; ai and email (which carries the sign-in codes and must not stop, #157) refuse Vedette's own ports on every address until the set is known (no AI or mail server listens on them). The SIEM save does not, because 514 and 6514 are every SIEM's ports; its socket refuses every send meanwhile. (4) **One sentence** for every refusal of Vedette itself, at save and at connect, in all four modules: "That address is Vedette itself: loopback, Vedette's own container, or one of its ports (8443, 8444, 8765, 514, 6514) on the machine that runs it. For another program on that machine, enter the machine's LAN address and that program's port." The hint is true on both install kinds now (the appliance's LAN address is allowed on other ports), so no install-kind branch is needed (finding 2 of walk 4); the other refusals keep their own sentences without "this machine". API error codes do not change (`blocked_host` for feeds, webhook and SIEM; `bad_host` for SMTP; `invalid_base_url` for AI). (5) **AI changes**: an internal profile at `localhost`/127.x is now refused at save, at test and at connect (it never reached anything but core in the container, D-226); a stored one stays loaded and its calls fail with the sentence. D-226's default `host.containers.internal` (the gateway, i.e. Ollama on the machine) keeps working, as does the walk-4 profile on the appliance's LAN address. (6) **Known limits**: the container's gateway is read from `/proc/net/route`, IPv4 only (Docker and Podman networks are IPv4 unless the operator turns IPv6 on; an IPv6 gateway is a deferred line). The machine's addresses are cached (vedette-host's answer 30 s, the alias names 30 s, served while a refresh runs, the first alias lookup at most 1 s in place), so a new address of the machine counts from the next refresh; the decoys are read at every check. A cloud AI profile behind the environment proxy is not judged at connect time (the dial goes to the proxy, which is the operator's), only at save. A decoy record that cannot be read counts as no decoys (they stay refused on Vedette's own ports through vedette-host's report). On a container-only install the gateway may also reach services the machine binds to the bridge (on Docker Desktop, `host.docker.internal` forwards to the machine's own localhost), as AI already allowed (D-226, D-422); the people who type these addresses are the box's admins. `core/conn` (connections) and the `response` webhook (Kiên's area) keep their own rules, which refuse the machine entirely; aligning them is a deferred line. The rule is a copy per module (feeds, notify/channel, logs, ai/provider), as `nat64Local` is, because the one shared place would be `core/` (Kiên's area). | Walk 4 (2026-11-13, appliance 192.168.18.141): `walk/w4/84-feed-added.txt`, `73-ai-added.txt`, `94-webhook-ownip.txt`; walk 3 (172.18.0.1 as the gateway). Top-tier: GitLab refuses webhook and integration requests to the local network, loopback and "the current GitLab instance server address" by default, with an admin switch and an allowlist, and never lifts the metadata block https://docs.gitlab.com/security/webhooks/ (a multi-tenant product where any maintainer adds hooks; Vedette's destinations are typed by its admins only); n8n's SSRF protection is off by default and, when on, blocks loopback and RFC 1918 with an allowlist https://docs.n8n.io/hosting/securing/ssrf-protection/ ; Grafana allows any data-source URL unless the admin sets `data_source_proxy_whitelist` https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/setup-grafana/configure-grafana/ ; Home Assistant's Ollama integration uses `http://localhost:11434` as its example https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/ollama/ (appliances that run helper services next to the main app reach them by the host's address). OWASP SSRF cheat sheet (judge the resolved address, block the application's own services) https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html . Chosen over **refuse the machine everywhere** (GitLab's default): it would turn off D-226's Ollama-on-the-same-machine default and the walk-4 AI profile, and on a container-only install it cannot be enforced anyway (core does not know the machine's LAN address, which is why the SMTP hint pointed there); what the machine's own address exposes beyond Vedette's ports is what every LAN device already reaches. Not chosen: an admin switch or allowlist (an option nobody asked for; ponytail), resolving names at save (D-420 (1)). | 2026-11-13 |
| D-447 | **Zalo personal is a real channel (still labelled experimental), with a real QR sign-in, a picked recipient and approvers who confirm a link sent to their Zalo while signed in as themselves.** This replaces D-369 (3) (Zalo personal sign-in kept experimental and moved after v1): kien tried it on 0.1.0-beta.1 and accepts it as a grey area (unofficial; Zalo may lock the account). (1) **QR sign-in**: Sign in with a QR code runs the Zalo web client's QR flow, re-implemented in Go from zca-js v2.2.0 `loginQR` (login page version, `logininfo`, `verify-client`, `authen/qr/generate`, the `waiting-scan` and `waiting-confirm` long polls, `checksession`, `jr.chat.zalo.me/jr/userinfo`, the device id `uuid-md5(userAgent)`), then one `getLoginInfo` with the new session; only then does the dialog say "Signed in as <account>". The session (cookies, imei, user agent) is the channel secret through `core/secrets`, saved by Save with `zalo_login`; the "I scanned it" button is gone. The QR image is decoded on the box and redrawn as an SVG path (no `data:` image under the page's CSP, and the browser never decodes Zalo's bytes). One sign-in per box at a time, in memory, 100 s for the code and 10 minutes for Save; at most one start per 30 s and five per hour. (2) **Recipient**: picked from the account's groups and friends (`getAllGroups` + `getGroupInfo`, `getAllFriends`), or found from a `zalo.me/g/…` invite link (`getGroupLinkInfo`; a group the account is not in is flagged) or a phone number (`findUser`); 20 look-ups per 10 minutes. Stored as before (numeric ID + group flag) plus the shown name. (3) **Approvers (option A, chosen by kien/supervisor after the Opus review found that a reply proves control of a Zalo account but not who the person is: a wrongly picked "Minh" would have become Bob's approver, breaking response INV-24)**: the administrator picks each approver's Zalo (a friend, or by phone number); on Save the box's account sends that Zalo a single-use confirm link `<BaseURL>/link/zalo?c=<token>` that names the Vedette user ("open this link and sign in to Vedette as Bob to link this Zalo account"). The token is made and kept by `response` (`ChatLinkToken`: an 8-hex hint of the person plus 128 random bits, stored hashed with (user, channel, Zalo ID), 10 minutes, single use, constant-time compare, five wrong tries, one a minute and five an hour per person, a new one replaces the old). Only the person, signed in to Vedette as themself, links it by pressing Confirm on `/link/zalo` (POST with CSRF to `/response/me/identities/zalo-personal/confirm`); opening the page never links; another signed-in user gets 403 `other_account` before anything is read, so the link stays good; a reply from the Zalo account links nothing (the reply-code link path of D-243, `LinkFromChat`/`Decisions.LinkChat`, is removed). An administrator's own row skips the message only when its address is the box's own signed-in Zalo account (the uid the saved session signs in as, which the QR sign-in proved): "Link my Zalo now" returns the same link and they confirm it in their session; any other Zalo of theirs gets the link by message like everyone's, so a wrongly picked friend can never become their identity (review round 2). Deleting the channel drops its approvers' proofs too. The confirm page shows the Zalo ID first and prominently, the admin-typed name only as "named … by your administrator". The dialog shows Sending → Waiting → Linked with Send again; audit `notify.zalo_link_code` (never the token), `response.identity_link`, and `notify.zalo_unlink` + `response.identity_unlink` when a linked approver is removed or given another Zalo (`response.DropChatLink`, so A→B→A needs a new confirmation); at most 10 link messages per 10 minutes per box. INV-24 holds: no administrator path marks a link for someone else. My account only shows Linked / Not linked for Zalo. zca-js has no sign-out call, so a cancelled, replaced or unsaved QR sign-in stays live on Zalo's side; the dialog says so. (4) **Warning**: one amber note line, not a red box. New hosts `id.zalo.me`, `chat.zalo.me`, `jr.chat.zalo.me` and the profile/friend services under `*.chat.zalo.me` are in PRIVACY.md flow 5 and Settings → Privacy. | kien's beta trial: the pasted/faked session did not work for an ordinary admin, the "numeric Zalo ID" field cannot be filled by ordinary users (a group invite link was pasted), and the approver step said "Enter the Zalo user ID" with nowhere to find it. Reading the protocol from its maintained source rather than guessing: zca-js v2.2.0 `src/apis/loginQR.ts`, `src/zalo.ts`, `getAllFriends.ts`, `getAllGroups.ts`, `getGroupInfo.ts`, `getGroupLinkInfo.ts`, `findUser.ts` (https://github.com/RFS-ADRENO/zca-js/tree/v2.2.0/src, fetched read-only 2026-11-13); the n8n Zalo community node signs in the same way. Unofficial-messenger bridges that lead their field sign in by scanning a QR code with the phone app and keep the resulting web session, e.g. mautrix-whatsapp (https://docs.mau.fi/bridges/go/whatsapp/authentication.html). Proving a contact address by a one-time secret sent to it, valid about 10 minutes, is the pattern of Twilio Verify (https://www.twilio.com/docs/verify); binding it to the signed-in account by a single-use link that must be opened while signed in as that user is how GitHub verifies an added email address (https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/setting-up-and-managing-your-personal-account-on-github/managing-email-preferences/verifying-your-email-address). A reply alone (option B) proves only control of the Zalo account, not who the person is, so it was dropped. The sources other than zca-js were not opened from this session (only the zca-js source was fetched). Rejected: a typed numeric ID for the recipient only (ordinary users cannot find it); keeping the sign-in in the client (the session would pass through the browser); a red warning box (kien: light, one line). | 2026-11-13 |
| D-449 | **The Email channel signs in with every common provider: presets, SMTP AUTH PLAIN/LOGIN, OAuth2 (XOAUTH2/OAUTHBEARER) for Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace without a browser; Gmail personal uses an app password (notify; S-NOT-1; kien 2026-11-13).** (1) **Presets** (`web/src/features/notify/emailProviders.ts`; the box knows only how each signs in, `channel.EmailAuth`): Custom SMTP; Gmail `smtp.gmail.com:587` STARTTLS, address + app password; Yahoo `smtp.mail.yahoo.com:465` TLS, app password; iCloud `smtp.mail.me.com:587` STARTTLS, full address + app-specific password; Zoho `smtp.zoho.com:465` TLS (paid org domains `smtppro.zoho.com`, other data centers: the server Zoho shows), password or app-specific password; Fastmail `smtp.fastmail.com:465` TLS, app password; SendGrid `smtp.sendgrid.net:587` STARTTLS, username literally `apikey`, password an API key; Mailgun `smtp.mailgun.org:587` STARTTLS (EU `smtp.eu.mailgun.org`), the domain's SMTP credentials (not the API key); Amazon SES `email-smtp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:587` STARTTLS (region in the name), SES SMTP credentials (not AWS access keys, one region); Postmark `smtp.postmarkapp.com:587` STARTTLS (465 not offered), the server API token as username and password (never stored as a field); Brevo `smtp-relay.brevo.com:587` STARTTLS, SMTP login + SMTP key; Microsoft 365 `smtp.office365.com:587` STARTTLS (Microsoft: 465 lacks the TLS versions it requires), OAuth2; Google Workspace `smtp.gmail.com:587` STARTTLS, OAuth2 service account. A preset fills host, port and encryption; they stay editable. (2) **SMTP AUTH**: PLAIN if offered, else LOGIN; with OAuth2 XOAUTH2, else OAUTHBEARER (RFC 7628); on a refusal the client answers the server's JSON challenge (empty line, or `%x01`) and the 535 comes back. The SASL code refuses to start on a connection that is not TLS, on top of the existing STARTTLS-required (587) and implicit TLS (465) rules; D-446 and the errors-under-the-field table stay. (3) **Microsoft 365**: client credentials to `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/oauth2/v2.0/token`, scope `https://outlook.office365.com/.default`; fields tenant ID (GUID or domain, the only configured part of the URL), client ID (GUID), client secret (the channel secret), mailbox (username). The dialog lists what the admin does once (SMTP.SendAsApp + admin consent, client secret, `New-ServicePrincipal` with the Enterprise application's Object ID, `Add-MailboxPermission … FullAccess`, SMTP AUTH on for the mailbox) with the doc link. Microsoft is ending Basic auth for SMTP AUTH (off by default for existing tenants at the end of December 2026), so the preset has no password mode. (4) **Google Workspace**: service account key file (JSON, the channel secret; only `type`, `client_email`, `private_key_id`, `private_key` read; `token_uri` ignored, the endpoint is fixed), RS256 JWT bearer grant (RFC 7523) with the Go standard library to `https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token`, `sub` = mailbox, scope `https://mail.google.com/`, one hour. (5) **Tokens**: fetched before the SMTP session opens (no session when the token service refuses), cached in memory per service until 5 minutes before expiry (key = hash of method, tenant, client, mailbox and secret), dropped when the SMTP server refuses it, never logged; token answers bounded (64 KiB, token ≤ 8 KiB printable ASCII), redirects never followed. Refusals are fixed sentences per OAuth error code (`invalid_client`, `unauthorized_client`, `invalid_grant`…); the provider's `error_description` and the SMTP server's text after an OAuth AUTH are never shown or logged. A saved secret is reused only with the same sign-in method (changing method without a new secret → `secret_required`). New codes `bad_provider`, `bad_tenant_id`, `bad_client_id`; `bad_secret` also for a key file or client secret of the wrong shape. (5b) **After the security review**: a saved secret is bound to the sign-in method, the server and the port (`fields.secret_for`, written by the box); changing any of them without a new secret is `secret_required`, or deletes the saved secret when the new configuration needs none ("No encryption"), so a client secret cannot be walked over to a password login in two saves and a password is never sent to a server it was not saved for. The OAuth presets accept only the provider's own SMTP server (`smtp.office365.com`, `smtp.gmail.com`): a `.default` token carries every permission of the app. Google keys are 2048–4096-bit RSA; passwords and usernames with control characters are refused under their field; token fetches are single-flight per key and the token cache is cleared when the email channel is saved or removed. The token requests skip D-446's connect-time check on purpose: their hosts are fixed public names. (6) **Gmail personal: app password, not browser OAuth.** Browser OAuth would need a redirect back to the box, and Google refuses raw IP hosts and non-HTTPS redirect URIs for web clients (the box is usually `https://192.168.x.y:8443`); the copy-paste (OOB) flow is gone since 2022/2023; `https://mail.google.com/` is a restricted scope, so a shared Vedette client would need Google's verification and a yearly security assessment, and each admin's own unverified "Testing" client gets refresh tokens that expire after 7 days. App passwords need 2-Step Verification, which the preset says, linking Google's app-password page. | Official pages: Google app passwords https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/185833 , Gmail SMTP https://support.google.com/mail/answer/7104828 ; Yahoo https://help.yahoo.com/kb/SLN4724.html ; iCloud https://support.apple.com/en-us/102525 ; Zoho https://www.zoho.com/mail/help/zoho-smtp.html ; Fastmail https://www.fastmail.help/hc/en-us/articles/1500000278342 ; SendGrid https://www.twilio.com/docs/sendgrid/for-developers/sending-email/integrating-with-the-smtp-api ; Mailgun https://documentation.mailgun.com/docs/mailgun/user-manual/sending-messages/send-smtp ; SES https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/smtp-connect.html , https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/smtp-credentials.html ; Postmark https://postmarkapp.com/developer/user-guide/send-email-with-smtp ; Brevo https://help.brevo.com/hc/en-us/articles/7924908994450 ; Microsoft 365 SMTP https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/exchange/mail-flow-best-practices/how-to-set-up-a-multifunction-device-or-application-to-send-email-using-microsoft-365-or-office-365 , OAuth for SMTP https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/exchange/client-developer/legacy-protocols/how-to-authenticate-an-imap-pop-smtp-application-by-using-oauth , SMTP AUTH per mailbox https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/exchange/clients-and-mobile-in-exchange-online/authenticated-client-smtp-submission , Basic auth timeline https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/exchange/updated-exchange-online-smtp-auth-basic-authentication-deprecation-timeline/4489835 (MC786329); RFC 7628 (OAUTHBEARER), RFC 7523 (JWT bearer). Top-tier for Gmail: Grafana (plain SMTP user/password, https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/setup-grafana/configure-grafana/#smtp ), Uptime Kuma (SMTP form, Gmail through an app password; no OAuth, https://github.com/louislam/uptime-kuma/blob/master/src/components/notifications/SMTP.vue ), Nextcloud (server email: password; Gmail OAuth only in the Mail app with an admin-created Google client, https://docs.nextcloud.com/server/latest/admin_manual/groupware/mail.html ), Zammad (Gmail OAuth with an admin-created Google Cloud web client and the instance's callback URL, https://admin-docs.zammad.org/en/latest/channels/google/basic-setup.html ).
