Not chosen: a password mode for Microsoft 365 (being retired), a Vedette-wide Google OAuth client (restricted-scope assessment, a project server, D-81), a device-code flow (Google does not allow the Gmail scope on it, https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/limited-input-device#allowedscopes ); D-480 later added user sign-ins with the customer's own client. | 2026-11-13 |
| D-450 | **vedette-host reports the IPv6 default routes, each default gateway's MAC and the DNS servers in use; response seeds them as never-touch, but only what core has seen stay put: new gateways, resolvers and gateway MACs are candidates for 10 minutes (closes the three limits of D-325).** `GET /v1/state/net` gains three optional fields, compatible both ways (no proto bump: core's client does not refuse unknown fields, and an older host simply sends none, so core seeds what D-325 seeded): (1) `resolvers[]`: the `nameserver` lines of `/run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf` (the servers systemd-resolved queries, a DHCP lease's included) **and** of `/etc/resolv.conf`, without loopback stubs (`127.0.0.53`, `::1`), unspecified or multicast addresses, zone dropped, deduplicated, at most 16; a file read (no exec). Both files: either may be what a program on the box uses. The host is root and `/run/systemd/resolve` belongs to `systemd-resolve` (review M2), so a file is read only when `lstat` says it is a regular file of 1 B to 64 KiB (procfs files report 0), opened with `O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK|O_NOCTTY`, and `fstat` is the same file; `/etc/resolv.conf` is followed one link level (Ubuntu's link to the stub; an absolute target is read under the root), never two, so a link to `/dev/watchdog` or `/proc/kmsg` is never opened. (2) `default_routes6[{iface, gateway, mac?}]`: every `::/0` route of `/proc/net/ipv6_route` with flags UP+GATEWAY and not REJECT and a unicast next hop (link-local is normal: a router advertisement's), the same next hop on the same card once, sorted by metric and then cut to the 16 lowest (review LOW 1, round 2); the file lists every routing table (VPN, VRF, policy) and each next hop of an equal-cost route on its own line. `gateway` is plain text with no zone and `iface` names the link. (3) `mac` on every route: the kernel's neighbour-table entry for the gateway **on the route's card**, in a state a neighbour answered with (REACHABLE, STALE, DELAY, PROBE, PERMANENT; not NOARP) with a 6-byte unicast non-zero address, read with one netlink `RTM_GETNEIGH` dump through the standard library (`syscall.NetlinkRIB`, the same kind of request the `net` package already makes for the interface list; `AF_NETLINK` is already in the unit's `RestrictAddressFamilies`); the parser is pure Go over the bytes, bounded (8 MiB, a length that does not fit ends the read) and fuzzed, one fuzz target against a reference of the rule. **Vetting in core (`hostMACs.vet`, reviews M1 of rounds 1 and 2)**: routes, resolv.conf and the neighbour table can all be steered by a host on the LAN (a rogue router advertisement or DHCP server, ARP/ND poisoning), and protecting an attacker's address or MAC makes the attacker untouchable, so it is not the safe direction. Hence: (a) the route gateways and resolvers of **core's first `state/net` answer after start** are trusted at once; (b) a gateway or resolver address **first seen later** is a candidate: neither its IP nor its MAC is seeded until it has been in **at least 3 answers in a row spanning at least 10 minutes** (an answer without it starts the count over); it is reported when its run starts (`network.gateway_new` / `network.dns_new`) and when it is adopted (`network.gateway_adopted` / `network.dns_adopted`); meanwhile a family (IPv4, IPv6) with no trusted gateway in the answer keeps its last gateways (carry-over, as for a lease being renewed), so a DHCP change of the gateway leaves the old one protected; (c) a trusted gateway's first MAC is pinned; a different MAC is a candidate under the same 3-answers/10-minutes rule, reported on change (`network.gateway_mac_changed`, at most once per 10 minutes per gateway) and on adoption (`network.gateway_mac_adopted`; adoptions are at least 10 minutes apart by construction); at most 4 pinned MACs per gateway and **the first pin is never dropped** (past 4 the second-oldest goes), so rotating MACs cannot push the real router's out (review M2, round 2); (d) what the administrator saved for the management card (netplan's gateway and DNS) is trusted at once, only the administrator writes it. Each report is a WARN line and a `core_audit` row (user `system`, target the address), written from its own goroutine because the report happens while response may hold the write transaction that asked for the list; its context is a 30 s timeout of its own, since `deps` carries no server-lifetime context (a row cut by a shutdown is lost, the WARN line is not). No new GUI surface (no story): the rows show in Settings → Audit log under the network group. Seeded entries: `response.HostInfra` with `MAC`, labelled "Default gateway of this box" / "DNS server of this box". An IPv6 link-local gateway is protected by its MAC only: response's IP type never accepts a link-local address, so no action can name one. | Why: D-325 left a DHCP box with only its gateway protected (the lease's resolvers were missing), an IPv6 gateway unprotected, and a MAC-only action (switch quarantine by MAC, an event with no IP) able to reach the gateway unless it was an inventory router. Same reasoning as D-325: pfSense's anti-lockout rule protects the box's own path without the admin listing it (https://docs.netgate.com/pfsense/en/latest/firewall/anti-lockout.html). Vetting follows arpwatch, which keeps the pairing it knows and reports "new station", "flip flop" and "changed ethernet address" rather than silently trusting a change (https://linux.die.net/man/8/arpwatch), and the RA Guard / DHCP snooping model, where only known router and server sources are trusted and new ones are not believed on sight (RFC 6105, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6105; Cisco Dynamic ARP Inspection: https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/switches/lan/catalyst9300/software/release/17-9/configuration_guide/sec/b_179_sec_9300_cg/configuring_dynamic_arp_inspection.html). Sources for where the data lives: systemd-resolved writes the upstream servers it uses to `/run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf` and the stub `127.0.0.53` to `stub-resolv.conf` (https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd-resolved.service.html, section "/etc/resolv.conf"); `/proc/net/ipv6_route` columns and `RTF_*` flags (`include/uapi/linux/ipv6_route.h`); neighbour dump and `NUD_*` states (`man 7 rtnetlink`, `include/uapi/linux/neighbour.h`). Not chosen: `resolvectl dns` or `ip -j neigh` through the exec allowlist (host-api §18 slice 3-3 keeps `ip`/`networkctl` out of the read path); `/proc/net/arp` for IPv4 plus netlink for IPv6 (two parsers where one dump answers both families); reading only `/etc/resolv.conf` (on Ubuntu it is the stub); only the lowest-metric IPv6 route (a VPN or policy table's gateway would be left out); seeding a new gateway, resolver or MAC at once (the rogue RA / DHCP / ARP case above) or never (a replaced router or a moved lease would stay unprotected for good). Limits: **a legitimate change of gateway or DNS by DHCP or a router advertisement is protected only after 10 minutes** (the old gateway stays protected meanwhile; a new DNS server is not); everything lives in core's memory, so whatever the first answer after a core start holds is trusted as it is, a rogue router or spoofed MAC active at that moment included, and so is the first MAC seen for an address adopted later; an attacker who keeps a rogue gateway, resolver or MAC up for 10 minutes without a gap is adopted (and has been reported twice by then); IPv4 still reads `/proc/net/route`, which lists the main table and the first next hop of a multipath route only; the whole neighbour dump is read (the kernel bounds it with `gc_thresh3`); a gateway the box has not talked to has no neighbour entry, so no MAC until it has; at most 32 addresses are remembered (past it, those not in the current answer are forgotten). | 2026-11-12 |
| D-451 | **Container-only release assets (WP-08m slice 7): every release that lists install mode `container` publishes `vedette.env`, `compose.yaml`, `compose.sensors.yaml` and `compose.syslog.yaml`, each with a `.minisig`, and the customer's update fetches and checks all four.** (1) **Builder**: `release container-assets -in release.in.json -out dist/release [-ref v<version>] [-compose-dir deploy/compose/container-only]` (`make release-container-assets`, between `release-manifest` and `release-sign`) reads the four files **from git at the release tag** (default `v<version>`, the same rule as the migrations of `manifest`: what is tagged is what ships, an edit left in the working tree never does), copies the compose files byte for byte, and fills only the three empty lines `VEDETTE_CORE_IMAGE=`, `VEDETTE_SENSOR_IMAGE=`, `VEDETTE_SCAN_IMAGE=` with the image digests of `release.in.json`, each exactly `ghcr.io/knt048/vedette-<service>@sha256:<64 hex>` (L5; never `:tag@`, because the Updates page checks the downloaded file with `grep -cF` for that text, `matchCmd`). It refuses: a missing or malformed digest or a release without the core, sensor or scan image; a value that fails that exact regex; a template image line that is not empty, missing or repeated; any other `*_IMAGE=` line (a fourth service added to compose without the builder); any change to another line (checked on the result, not assumed); a file that does not start with a `#` comment line (nothing signed with the release key may look like a JSON document or a content statement, D-346); install modes that are empty, unknown or repeated (also refused by `manifest` now, before the box's verifier would); and **install modes without `container`**: assets published for a release no container install is offered would only mislead. (2) **Signing**: `release sign` signs the four files next to the manifest, in the active and rescue slots (never the backup slot), with the trusted comment `file:<name> version:<manifest version>`, so `minisign -V` shows the customer which release a signed file belongs to (a replayed compose file of an older release shows as such); all four or none, and never next to an index-only refresh. Same pinned minisign and key as the documents (`scripts/release/minisign.sh`, `sign.go`). (3) **Verify both ways**: `release verify` requires, when the manifest lists `container`, all four files and signatures, each passing `release.VerifyContent`, signed by the manifest's own key, with this release's trusted comment, and `vedette.env` naming exactly the manifest's core, sensor and scan pull references; when the manifest does not list `container`, any of the four files is refused. So a release that offers container-only installs cannot be published without the files the page tells customers to download (LOW-6), and the first real release's `release.in.json` lists `"install_modes": ["appliance", "container"]` (Makefile flow comment; `scripts/testchannel` already does). `internal/release` is unchanged. (4) **Update steps on the page and in `docs/INSTALL-CONTAINER.md` §5** (LOW-4): keep = `mkdir vedette-<running> && mv -n vedette.env compose.yaml compose.sensors.yaml compose.syslog.yaml vedette-<running>/` (a NEW folder named after the running release: `mkdir` without `-p` refuses an existing one and then a labelled block puts its files back before moving it aside, `cp vedette-<running>/* .` then `mv vedette-<running> vedette-<running>-before` (QA r2: renaming alone after a stopped update would keep the unchecked new files as the way back), so a kept way back is never mixed with other files; `mv -n` never overwrites); fetch = `u=https://github.com/KNT048/vedette/releases/download/v<new>` and one `curl -fsSLO` loop for the four files and their signatures that stops at the first failure (`|| { echo "download failed: $f"; break; }`; the release assets, where `install.sh` and the box already download from, D-150); verify = one loop `[ "$(minisign -VQm "$f" -p vedette.pub)" = "file:$f version:<new>" ] && echo "$f ok" || { echo "$f FAILED: stop"; break; }` with the key kept from the install in the same folder (review r1 M1: `-Q` prints only the trusted comment, measured with the pinned 0.12 in `TestInteropMinisignCLI`; comparing it exactly refuses a signed file of another release and a signature of another file, e.g. sensors and syslog swapped, which a plain `-V` passes); then cosign and the `grep -cF` count as before (only a known service with a `sha256:<64 hex>` digest goes into a command line); the customer's two lines are copied from `vedette-<running>/vedette.env`, and the text before the pull block gives the exact `-f compose.yaml -f compose.sensors.yaml -f compose.syslog.yaml` form for those who run the add-ons (the page cannot tell which overlays a customer started); "If any check fails, stop and put your files back" and the way back is its own copyable block, `cp vedette-<running>/* .` then `pull` and `up -d` (Docker or Podman); every block has a label. A running or offered version that does not fit `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9.+-]{0,63}$` gets no commands at all, only a pointer to §5 (no placeholder to fix by hand). With no release offered, the page says its `pull`/`up -d` block re-pulls what `vedette.env` names and never moves to a new release. The guide's §1 starts with an empty folder that holds the two keys, the release files and later the kept folders. Confirmed in `docs/INSTALL-CONTAINER.md` before relying on it: the customer's settings are only `VEDETTE_BIND_IP` and `VEDETTE_HOSTS` of `vedette.env` (§2, "the one file you edit"; the compose files take everything else from it), and §2 now says not to edit the compose files because an update replaces them. (5) **Keys in the guide**: the real keys exist (D-256), so the guide gives them, to be saved once as `vedette.pub` and `cosign.pub` from the repository, not from the release page; `TestInstallGuideKeysAreTheEmbeddedOnes` keeps the guide equal to the keys compiled in. The download URL is the real release-asset URL; no release is published yet (WP-08k), and the guide says so. | Why: the update replaced only `vedette.env`, so a release that changed a compose file (a new flag, a limit, a mount) never reached a container-only customer (LOW-4), and nothing tied the manifest's `install_modes` to files that exist (LOW-6). How others do it: **authentik** tells compose users to download the latest `compose.yml` on every upgrade, then `docker compose pull` and `up -d`, after a database backup, and does not support downgrades (https://docs.goauthentik.io/install-config/upgrade/); **Immich** publishes `docker-compose.yml` and `example.env` as GitHub release assets (`wget -O docker-compose.yml https://github.com/immich-app/immich/releases/latest/download/docker-compose.yml`, https://docs.immich.app/install/docker-compose/), upgrades with `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d`, and changes the compose file only when the release notes say so (https://docs.immich.app/install/upgrading/); **Nextcloud AIO** updates its containers from its own mastercontainer, which needs the Docker socket, and asks for a backup before "Start and update containers" (https://github.com/nextcloud/all-in-one#how-to-update-the-containers). Chosen: authentik's "replace the compose file on every update" (no change can be missed) with Immich's place (GitHub release assets, settings in the env file), plus what neither has: a minisign signature per file checked with a key kept from the install, the release named in the signed comment, and the old files kept for the way back (authentik and Immich overwrite them). Not chosen: Immich's "edit compose only when the notes say" (a missed note leaves an old compose); a mastercontainer with the Docker socket (root on the customer's machine, against D-168's no-helper design); "download from the release page" without a command (the machine is usually a headless server, and the earlier page had no address because the assets did not exist yet); a tarball of the four files (one more tool and format to verify for no gain); one signature over a list of hashes (the customer would have to compute and compare hashes by hand); refusing an appliance-only release (a host-only hotfix is legitimate: it just publishes no container files). Limits: a rescue release (D-259) signs the four files with the backup key, which a customer's `vedette.pub` (the active key) does not verify; that customer follows the rescue notes. The `curl` loop needs a POSIX shell (not fish). `scripts/testchannel` publishes no container assets, so a container-only lab box offered a test release would get 404 at the download step (deferred). | 2026-11-12 |
| D-452 | **`container.pull` with `source: bundle` loads the image from the offline bundle core uploaded, verified exactly like a registry pull, and ends on the registry path unchanged (replaces `412 bundle_unsupported`).** (1) **Where the bundle is**: core streams the upload to `<core_data>/bundles/<bundle_id>.tar`; `bundle_id` is 32 random lowercase hex chosen by core (like a `snapshot` id or a `host-packages/<id>.deb`), not a hash of the tar (core would read 8 GiB to name it, and the host trusts no hash core computed). The host builds the name from the id, opens it through core's tree (INV-14: `os.Root`, the descriptor must be a regular file owned by `core_uid` with one link, at most 8 GiB, not a symlink, `O_NONBLOCK`), and never takes a path. Missing → `412 bundle_not_found`; anything else wrong → `412 bundle_invalid`. Core removes the file afterwards; the host never writes or deletes in `bundles/`. (2) **The tar is untrusted and never extracted by name**: headers are read (members skipped by seeking), the names are a closed list (`bundle.json`, `index.json` + `.minisig`, `release-manifest.json` + `.minisig`, `sbom.json`, `images/<service>.oci.tar` for the five services, `host/<name>.deb`, and the folders `images/` and `host/`), regular files and those two folders only (no link, hard link, device, FIFO or sparse entry), no duplicate, at most 64 entries, each under its cap (256 KiB a document, 2 KiB a signature, 1 MiB `bundle.json`, 64 MiB `sbom.json`, 256 MiB a `.deb`). The four documents are read into memory; `bundle.json`, `sbom.json` and `host/*.deb` are allowed but not read by the host. (3) **Verification**: the documents go through the very same `verifyPull` (same refusals, same order, all in `Check`; the bundle's index is stored like a sent one, sequence never goes back, expiry only warns, so a stale index is accepted with `index_expired`); the request carries no documents (`400` if it does: one source of truth). Then the bundle must hold `images/<service>.oci.tar` (`bundle_invalid`), and `low_disk` asks for **3 × the archive's size** free both where images live and in the host's state (the staged copy, then Podman's copy and unpacked layers). In the run, the archive (an OCI image layout as a tar) is copied into a fresh `0700` directory `<state>/bundle/img-*`: only `oci-layout`, `index.json` and `blobs/sha256/<64 hex>` (the latter written to new files and hashed while written; at most 4096 blobs); the archive's `index.json` must name **exactly one** image whose digest is the **signed** one (`images[].digest`, the multi-platform index digest); that blob, the platform manifest for `linux/<arch>` it lists, and that manifest's config and layers must be there at their declared sizes. A blob that does not hash to its name, or another digest → run `failed` `archive_digest_mismatch`; a missing piece, a link, an unknown name → `failed` `bundle_invalid`. The cosign check is `VerifyImage` on the signed digest, which the archive now provably is. (4) **Loading**: the host writes the layout's `index.json` itself (the verified descriptor, annotated `org.opencontainers.image.ref.name=ghcr.io/knt048/vedette-<service>:<version>`) and runs `podman pull -q oci:<dir>:ghcr.io/knt048/vedette-<service>:<version>` (a new fixed argv shape, `validBuildDir` + `release.ImageRef`). Measured on Podman 5.7.0 here (offline, a two-platform list built with buildah): the image is stored as `ghcr.io/knt048/vedette-<service>:<version>`, `Digest` = the index digest, `RepoDigests` holds `ghcr.io/knt048/vedette-<service>@<index digest>`, so `image inspect <pull ref>` answers as after a registry pull and the existing `inspect` → `tag localhost/…` → `inspect` → record path, the scan build (`--pull=never`, `BASE_IMAGE=<pull ref>`), `container.start`, `rollback` and retention (`ownedName` accepts the tag) run unchanged. Idempotent: an image already here with the right digest is not copied or loaded (signatures still checked). The layout is removed right after the load, at the next bundle pull and at `Start`. Timeout unchanged (45 min; the copy of 8 GiB is minutes). (5) **`host/*.deb` is not `container.pull`'s**: `host.self_update` (D-316) already reads the package core wrote at `<core_data>/host-packages/<id>.deb` and checks its SHA-256 against the signed manifest, so core extracts the `.deb` from the bundle to that place and calls `host.self_update` with the bundle's four documents: no host change, no silent change to self_update. (6) **Builder rule** (update-manifest §11): each `images/<service>.oci.tar` is an OCI layout tar whose `index.json` names exactly one image, the digest of `images[].digest`, exported with digests preserved (`skopeo copy --all --preserve-digests docker://ghcr.io/knt048/vedette-<s>@<digest> oci-archive:…` or `podman manifest push --all`); at least the `linux/<arch>` platforms the manifest lists. | Why: the bundle is the only update path of an air-gapped box, and its trust must come from the release signatures alone (§11), with the same checks as online so there is one verifier. Top-tier air-gap installs ship images as archives that the node imports locally rather than a registry mirror: RKE2 and k3s read image tarballs dropped into `agent/images/` (https://docs.rke2.io/install/airgap, https://docs.k3s.io/installation/airgap), Harbor's offline installer ships the images as a tarball loaded with the engine (https://goharbor.io/docs/main/install-config/download-installer/), and Zarf packages store images as an OCI image layout inside a signed package and check every blob by digest before use (https://docs.zarf.dev/ref/packages/). Signed-bundle appliances verify the signature before anything is installed (RAUC, used by Home Assistant OS: https://rauc.readthedocs.io/en/latest/basic.html). The OCI layout is content-addressed (https://github.com/opencontainers/image-spec/blob/main/image-layout.md), so hashing each blob against its name and walking from the signed digest proves the content without trusting the archive's own index. Not chosen: `podman load -i` (names the image from the archive's unsigned annotation, and its output must be parsed); `podman pull oci-archive:<path>` (Podman extracts the whole tar again into `/var/tmp`, a third copy, and also names from the annotation: https://github.com/containers/image/blob/main/docs/containers-transports.5.md); passing core's file to Podman (core owns the inode and could rewrite it after the check); extracting the outer tar to disk (only the one image is needed, and nothing is written by a name from the tar); a host-side `bundle.json` check (unsigned; every byte the host uses is signed or hashed against something signed); `bundle_id` = hash of the tar (see (1)). After security review r1: core owns the file and can rewrite it after the 202, so the run measures the free space again for the size Check saw and refuses an image archive of any other size (`bundle_invalid`), and both tar readers refuse sparse entries (Go's archive/tar expands a PAX `GNU.sparse.*` entry into a plain file of its `realsize`, so a few hundred bytes would read back as GiBs) and require the members to claim no more than the file holds (overflow-safe sum). Blobs the verified chain does not reference are not refused: an index's other platforms are legitimately unreferenced by this machine's chain, and the total written is now bounded by a size measured twice. Limits: the scan image still needs Debian's mirror for its on-box nmap build (D-147), so on a box with no internet a bundle pull of `scan` ends `scan_build_failed` (the base stays loaded and tagged); Podman 4.9.3 (Ubuntu 24.04) and the real ghcr.io export are not yet run in the lab (deferred); the layout holds every platform's blobs of the archive, not only this machine's; a bundle's tag `ghcr.io/knt048/vedette-<service>:<version>` stays on the image until retention removes it. | 2026-11-12 |
| D-453 | **vedette-host never reboots while a logind block inhibitor of shutdown is held (apt installing): it reads logind's lock list itself before every reboot and refuses, waits or reports instead.** Measured on Debian 13.7 and Ubuntu 26.04.1: while apt installs, APT holds a logind lock ("APT is installing or removing packages", what `shutdown` / `shutdown:sleep`, mode `block`, uid 0), and `systemctl reboot` from a system service fails with "Operation denied due to active block inhibitor"; before this the host only logged it while `os.reboot now` had already answered `succeeded`, and a scheduled reboot was dropped, so the box silently did not reboot. **logind enforces this for root only from systemd 257** (Debian 13, Ubuntu 26.04). On systemd 255 (Ubuntu 24.04, a supported platform) `logind_check_inhibitors` returns at once for euid 0 and `verify_shutdown_creds` ignores locks of the caller's own uid, and APT's lock is uid 0 like the host, so logind lets the reboot through and it cuts dpkg: there the host's own read is the only guard (review M1, round 1). (1) **Reading the locks**: `busctl --system --json=short call org.freedesktop.login1 /org/freedesktop/login1 org.freedesktop.login1.Manager ListInhibitors`, one new exact argv in the exec allowlist (`/usr/bin/busctl`, systemd package, already a Depends); `--json` exists since systemd 240 (Ubuntu 24.04 has 255, Debian 13 257, Ubuntu 26.04 259). A lock blocks a reboot when its mode is exactly `block` and `shutdown` is one of its `what` words; `delay` (unattended-upgrades' shutdown hook) never refuses, and `block-weak` (systemd 257) is ignored by logind for root. The parser is fail-closed: exactly `{"type":"a(ssssuu)","data":[[[what,who,why,mode,uid,pid],...]]}`, no unknown field, no trailing data, at most 8192 locks and 1 MiB, otherwise the list is **unknown**, never partial. `who`/`why` come from any local program: printable ASCII only without quotes, angle brackets, ampersand, backquote or backslash (others become `?`), spaces collapsed, at most 64/120 bytes, no trailing space. One read takes at most 3 s inside `os.reboot`'s Check (the server bounds a Check at 5 s) and 10 s elsewhere. (2) **Unknown means allow, logged once** (WARN on the first unknown after a good read): on systemd 257+ logind still refuses a locked reboot; **on 255 an unknown list means the host reboots without protection from apt**, as every release before this one did. Refusing on unknown would leave the box unable to reboot whenever busctl or its output breaks. The output shape is confirmed: on Ubuntu 24.04 (systemd 255.4-1ubuntu8.18) by the lead's lab on 2026-11-12, while apt-get installed and at idle (`host/ops/testdata/inhibitors_systemd255_apt.json`: APT's row `["shutdown","APT","APT is installing or removing packages","block",0,5068]` is the one block shutdown lock), and on systemd 259 (`inhibitors_systemd259.json`); the Debian 13 (257) shape is still part of the lab check. (3) **`os.reboot now`**: `Check` refuses with a new `409 reboot_inhibited` whose message names who and why. (4) **Before every `systemctl reboot`** (a "now" reboot, a scheduled one, every retry) the host reads the list again; a lock there means no call, and the wait below. (5) **Scheduled reboot**: when its time comes, the list is read first, outside the reboot mutex and before the write gate goes up; a lock postpones it like a running command (`rebootRetryBusy`, 1 minute), the schedule stays (`reboot_scheduled_at`), `reboot_waiting_inhibitor` is audited once per schedule, and the existing 24-hour expiry bounds the wait. (6) **The wait of a started reboot** (a lock seen just before the call, or `systemctl reboot` refused by logind with a lock in the list read again; systemctl's localized stderr is never parsed): tries again every 30 s for up to 30 minutes from the start, raising the `rebooting` write gate again at every try so nothing new starts (`os.reboot.cancel` included), audits the wait once, then gives up with `reboot_failed` `{reason: inhibited, who, why}`, clears `Pending` and lowers the gate; any other failure is `reboot_failed` `{reason: systemctl_failed}` at once, as before. (7) **Host restart during the wait**: `reboot.json`'s pending reboot carries `issued` (set once `systemctl reboot` is accepted). A host start on the same boot keeps the gate only for an issued reboot younger than 10 minutes (the box is shutting down); any other same-boot pending reboot is audited `reboot_failed` `{reason: host_restarted, issued}` and cleared, never re-armed, so no later boot reports a misleading `reboot_completed`. (8) **Never** `--check-inhibitors=no`, `--force` or `-i`; and **not** `--check-inhibitors=yes` either: on 255 it also refuses while another user has a session open, which an admin's SSH login always is. (9) **Core and GUI**: no change in this PR; they learn only from the host's audit and log today. Spec text (host-api §6.4) and a deferred line describe the follow-up: core maps `reboot_inhibited` to a 409 with the host's cleaned text, and `GET /v1/state/os` gains `reboot_wait` and `reboot_failed` for the Updates page. | Why: rebooting while dpkg configures can leave packages half-configured; the lead's lab showed `systemctl reboot --force` cutting dpkg mid-configure, which the self-update applier survived but other apt runs may not, and Ubuntu runs unattended-upgrades by default, so a night reboot can meet apt. Nobody in the reference set forces past the lock: systemd says a block lock "inhibits operations entirely until the lock is released" and only a privileged user may override it (https://systemd.io/INHIBITOR_LOCKS/); APT takes the lock precisely so that halts and reboots wait for package operations (Ubuntu bug 1820886, https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/apt/+bug/1820886); unattended-upgrades' `Automatic-Reboot` runs `/sbin/shutdown -r <time>` after its own run with no flag to ignore inhibitors and only logs when it fails (https://github.com/mvo5/unattended-upgrades/blob/master/unattended-upgrade, `schedule_shutdown`). The root exemption of systemd 255 is the reviewer's reading of `logind_check_inhibitors` and `verify_shutdown_creds` in systemd v255 (review M1); the lead checks it on an Ubuntu 24.04 VM. The lead's brief also names Synology DSM and pfSense/OPNsense refusing a reboot while their own update runs and needrestart, which restarts services and leaves reboots to the admin; not re-verified here, and none of them is cited as forcing. Not chosen: `systemd-inhibit --list` (no JSON even in systemd 259, free-text columns that cannot be split reliably); speaking D-Bus in Go (a new dependency for one read-only call); parsing systemctl's stderr (localized and not a contract); `systemctl --check-inhibitors=yes` (above); refusing on an unknown list (above); retrying a "now" reboot forever (the gate would block core's writes indefinitely); re-arming a waiting reboot after a host restart (the caller who asked for it may be gone; reporting is safer than rebooting later on a stale request). Limits: on 255 a lock taken between the host's last read and logind's handling of the call (milliseconds) is not seen; on 255 an unknown list gives no protection; a lock held for more than 30 minutes after a "now" reboot ends in `reboot_failed`, and the operator reboots again; a scheduled reboot that waits longer than 24 hours expires (`reboot_schedule_expired`); `who`/`why` text that is not ASCII shows as `?`; the result depends on apt taking the lock (APT has done so since at least 1.6.11, per the bug above). | 2026-11-12 |
| D-454 | **The `scan-base` image ships the licences of the Go modules linked into nuclei, and `scripts/hostlicenses` gets exactly one exception to "a linked module without a licence file fails": `github.com/censys/censys-sdk-go` at v0.19.1 only, treated as MIT on the author's word.** (1) **Exception** (`noLicenseFile` in `scripts/hostlicenses/main.go`, keyed `path@version`): used only when the module directory has no licence file; it ships the standard MIT text (https://opensource.org/license/mit) with the copyright line "Copyright (c) Censys, Inc." (upstream names no holder or year; Censys, Inc. publishes the repository) under the heading `github.com/censys/censys-sdk-go v0.19.1 (MIT per the README, https://github.com/censys/censys-sdk-go/blob/v0.19.1/README.md; upstream has no LICENSE file)`. The README at that tag carries the "License: MIT" badge linked to opensource.org/licenses/MIT; neither the tag nor `main` has a LICENSE file (checked 2026-11-12 through the GitHub API; GitHub detects no licence). Any other module without a licence file, and any other version of this one, still fails; a module listed there that does have a licence file ships its own file (tests `TestNoLicenseFileException`). (2) **Image**: the `build` stage also compiles `scripts/hostlicenses` for the build machine (`/tools/hostlicenses`); the `nuclei` stage copies it and runs it inside the unpacked nuclei source over `./cmd/nuclei` with the target GOOS/GOARCH, `CGO_ENABLED=0 GOTOOLCHAIN=local GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly GOPROXY=off`, so the list comes from the same `go.sum` and the modules the build has just fetched, with no network. The result ships as `nuclei-third-party-licenses` next to `nuclei-LICENSE.md`, in `/usr/local/share/vedette/licenses/` and `/usr/share/doc/vedette/` (the vedette-sensor list stays `third-party-licenses`). `deploy/containers` tests hold the Containerfile to it; `make images-check` checks by effect that both files hold nuclei's own licence and the censys section. (3) **Upstream**: a request for a LICENSE file is drafted, not sent (issues are disabled on the repository and CONTRIBUTING.md accepts no pull requests); when a tagged version has the file, the entry is removed. | Why: since D-319 nuclei is built from source, so the image redistributes its ~380 modules and the MIT/BSD/Apache texts they require must travel with it; the only module without a file was censys-sdk-go. Debian and Fedora accept a licence stated by the author outside a licence file and package it with the standard text while asking upstream to add the file: Fedora "Identifying licenses" lists "a statement in a README" as a valid source of licence information (https://docs.fedoraproject.org/en-US/legal/identify/); Debian Policy 12.5 requires the licence text in `debian/copyright` (https://www.debian.org/doc/debian-policy/ch-docs.html#copyright-information), which packagers fill with the standard text of the licence upstream states. Not chosen: dropping the rule for all modules (a new unlicensed dependency would ship silently); a path-only exception (a later version could change licence unseen); waiting for upstream (no channel with a known answer time, and the image would keep shipping without the texts); patching censys out of nuclei (changes the program, D-319 keeps the Go sources unmodified). Limits: the copyright holder line is ours, not upstream's; only the README states the licence. | 2026-11-12 |
| D-455 | **vedette-host adds a host port to a unit only at a restart it checks, and refuses one that is busy before it touches the running release (host, S-CORE-2, S-CORE-7; follows D-395 and D-214, D-316 (10)).** (1) **Gap**: D-395 adds `PublishPort=127.0.0.1:8765:8765` to core's unit, D-214 added `6514`. `install.sh` refuses a busy port on a fresh box, but an update in place never runs it: if another program listens on 8765, the new core unit cannot reserve the port, core does not start, and 8443 is gone until the revert. (2) **A change that only takes effect at a later restart never adds a host port** (same port and protocol as the unit on disk, any address): the unit migration at host start (D-316 (10)) runs at boot, before the programs that may hold the port have bound it, and its text would take effect at the next restart with no check and no health revert behind it; so it keeps the earlier unit whenever the current template adds a port, busy or not, with one `container.start unit_migration_deferred` audit line (`service`, `digest`, `ports`) per host start. A `container.start` without `restart` of a running, healthy service keeps its unit's template too (only `[Install]` may come back, from that same template), succeeds and audits the same line with `run_id`; `container.stop persist` drops `[Install]` from the unit's own template. (3) **The restart checks**: `container.start` with `restart` or another digest, and `container.rollback`, refuse **`412 port_in_use`** at `Check` when a new port is busy, again in `Run` right before the transition journal, and for a version switch once more right before the unit is written (after the `pre_update` backup, which can take minutes; the journal is dropped, the backup stays). A stopped service (`inactive`, `failed`) holds no port, so in `Run` every port of its unit is looked at; a running one, only the new ports (its container holds the others). The message names each port and the process (`8765/tcp (python3, pid 4242)`); the restart keeps its health revert. A `container.start` without `restart` and without a new digest is judged in `Run`, once the host knows whether it restarts. (4) **How it looks**: the kernel's socket tables `/proc/net/{tcp,tcp6,udp,udp6}` (TCP in LISTEN, every bound UDP socket; a clash is the same address, or either side unspecified, `::` counting for IPv4 because the table does not show `IPV6_V6ONLY`), and, only for a clashing socket, `/proc/<pid>/fd` links `socket:[inode]` with the holder's `comm` (printable ASCII, 15 characters) and `cgroup`. A socket held by a process of the service's own systemd unit (`/system.slice/vedette-<service>.service` or below: its conmon, its container) is not a conflict. `PublishPort=` is read only in the forms the host writes (`[ip:]host:container[/tcp|/udp]`); a range, a missing host port or another protocol is skipped, and a test pins that every line of every template is read. No program runs, no socket is opened, no probe bind. A table that cannot be read (also a read error half way) is logged and refuses nothing: the revert path stays the safety net, and the check never blocks an update on its own misreading. (5) **Consequence**: a template with a new port reaches a box only through core's restart of the service (the image step of a software run), never through a reboot. Core's update run gets the code as a final refusal of the step; its user-facing sentence is core's (deferred). | Why: the failure mode is the one Docker Compose shows when it recreates a container whose port was taken ("port is already allocated" after the old container is gone): the old release is down before the conflict is known. Top-tier installers and orchestrators check host ports **before** they act: kubeadm's preflight refuses `init`/`join`/`upgrade` when a control-plane port is in use (https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/setup-tools/kubeadm/implementation-details/#preflight-checks), and the Kubernetes scheduler's `NodePorts` filter does not place a pod whose `hostPort` is taken on that node (https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/scheduling/config/#scheduling-plugins). systemd and Podman have no such preflight: a `PublishPort=` that cannot bind makes the Quadlet unit fail at start (https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-systemd.unit.5.html), so the host has to look itself, and only at the moment it acts, which is why a change that acts later (boot) does not get a port at all. Reading `/proc/net/tcp` and `/proc/<pid>/fd` is what `ss -p`, `netstat -p` and `lsof` do (https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/proc_net_tcp.html, https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc_pid_fd.5.html). Not chosen: checking the port in the migration at boot (first draft; the Opus review found it races the programs that bind later, and a failure then has no revert); a probe bind (`net.Listen`, kubeadm's way): the host may not open a network socket (FORBID-2), and a bind on 127.0.0.1 says nothing about a listener on another address; running `ss` (an external program for what two file reads give); checking every port of a running service with the owner rule only (a cgroup layout we did not foresee for conmon would refuse every update); refusing on an unreadable table (one odd `/proc` would block updates for good). | 2026-11-12 |
| D-456 | **Box without Docker: `vedette-int.network` gets no `isolate` option (neither `true` nor `strict`); nothing changes for new or installed boxes (closes the D-396 deferred line "netavark isolates only with `isolate`").** What the option does, from netavark's own firewall code (`src/firewall/nft.rs`, v1.14; the iptables driver of 1.4 has the same chains): FORWARD jumps to `NETAVARK-ISOLATION-1`, which matches only packets that **leave** an isolated bridge (`iifname <bridge> oifname != <bridge>`); with `isolate=true` they are dropped only when they go out to another bridge that is also isolated, with `strict` when they go out to any netavark bridge; every drop matches a netavark bridge by name, never a card or a bridge of the box (`br-lan`). (1) `isolate=true` closes nothing: a customer's Podman network made without the option (every network by default up to netavark 1.x, the `podman` default network included) is not isolated, so its packets to `vedette-int` never enter the isolation chains and the replies go back to a non-isolated bridge. (2) `strict` would block TCP from those networks in effect (the replies leaving `vedette0` hit the drop, which stands above netavark's `ct state established` accept), but not a one-way UDP packet; it is unknown to netavark 1.4 of Ubuntu 24.04 (`strict` came in 1.7; 26.04 ships 1.16, Debian 13 1.14), so the network file would differ per OS for a partial gain. (3) Netavark 2.0 makes `strict` the default for every bridge network ("to restore the previous behavior the network must set `isolate=false`"), so a supported OS that ships it isolates `vedette-int` with no change of ours. Vedette's own paths stay: on `vedette-int` stand only `core` (published 8443, 127.0.0.1:8444, 514, 6514) and the on-box scan build (`--network vedette-int`, needs the internet through the box's uplink, not another netavark bridge); `sensor` and `scan` use the host's network, the honeypot its own namespace `vedette-hp` (`Network=ns:`), the LAN comes in through a card and the box's uplink bridges are not netavark's, so no isolation chain matches them. **One path does break:** a customer's root Podman container on another netavark network can no longer reach core's published 8443, 514 or 6514 through the box's address. By 1.14's chains (if 2.0 keeps them), the FORWARD jump to `NETAVARK-ISOLATION-1` stands above every network's `ct state related,established accept`, so the DNAT'd packet that leaves a strict customer bridge for `vedette0` is dropped, and with the customer's `isolate=false` the replies leaving a strict `vedette0` are dropped. Only Vedette can set `isolate=false` on `vedette-int`, and even that leaves a strict customer network cut off (strict drops toward non-isolated bridges too). Whether that path matters, and whether `vedette-int` then needs `isolate=false`, is decided when a supported OS ships netavark ≥ 2.0 (deferred line, install-check on that OS). (4) An installed network cannot take the option in place: Quadlet makes it with `podman network create --ignore`, which leaves an existing network's configuration as it is, and `podman network update` changes only DNS servers; it would need core stopped, `podman network rm vedette-int` and a new create (a short outage of core, same subnet). Since nothing is added, no migration is needed. What stays open on a box without Docker: a customer's other root Podman containers (and any root process of the box, as before) can open a port of `core` on `vedette-int` that is not published to them, notably 8444 that is published only on 127.0.0.1; closing that needs a forward rule like D-396 (b) in a firewall that is not Docker's, which D-267 rules out, so it waits for netavark 2 (deferred line: install-check on the first supported OS with netavark ≥ 2.0). Rejected: `isolate=true` (closes nothing, see (1)); `strict` where netavark ≥ 1.7 (two forms of the network file, a recreate for installed boxes, partial, and the default anyway from netavark 2.0); our own nftables rule on boxes without Docker (a firewall Vedette does not own, D-267). | Sources: Podman, [podman-network-create(1), latest](https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-network-create.1.html) (`strict`: block traffic to and from all other bridge networks, the default when the option is omitted; `true`: only between networks that both have isolation; `false` restores the pre-Podman 6 / Netavark 2 behaviour; `--ignore` does not change an existing network) and [v4.9.3](https://docs.podman.io/en/v4.9.3/markdown/podman-network-create.1.html) / [v5.4.2](https://docs.podman.io/en/v5.4.2/markdown/podman-network-create.1.html) (isolation only between networks that have the option); netavark, [firewall/nft.rs v1.14.0](https://github.com/containers/netavark/blob/v1.14.0/src/firewall/nft.rs) (ISOLATION-1/2/3 chains, the jump above the established accept); netavark [release notes](https://docs.rs/crate/netavark/1.10.3/source/RELEASE_NOTES.md) (isolate in v1.1.0, `isolate=strict` in v1.7.0) and [v2.0.0](https://newreleases.io/project/github/containers/netavark/release/v2.0.0) (strict isolation by default); [Ubuntu netavark](https://launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/netavark) (noble 1.4.0, resolute 1.16.1), [Debian trixie netavark](https://packages.debian.org/trixie/netavark) (1.14.0); Quadlet dry run on Podman 5.7 (`ExecStart=… podman network create --ignore --subnet … --interface-name=vedette0 vedette-int`). | 2026-11-12 |
| D-457 | **WP-08k release job: images are pushed and recorded by digest (`release-push` → `dist/release/images.json`), the release description is generated (`release-in`), and GitHub release assets are published draft-first, every asset and image checked as a box sees it, with the fixed `index` release uploaded last and only onto the index the release was built on (`release-publish`); order and owners in `docs/plans/2026-11-12-wp08k-release-job.md`.** (1) **Push** (`scripts/release push`, podman only, fixed argv, no shell): the four manifest lists of `make images` (`localhost/vedette-{core,sensor,scan-base,honeypot}:<version>`; `scan-base` is published as `vedette-scan`, the name the manifest, cosign identity and `vedette.env` use); every platform image must carry `org.opencontainers.image.version=<version>`; a local image named like the remote is refused (podman reads local storage first and `manifest inspect` has no `docker://` form, measured with 5.7); a version tag already in the registry is compared anonymously, platform by platform, by config digest with the local images: the same → reused, other → refused (a pushed version is never replaced); otherwise `podman manifest push --all --compression-format=gzip --digestfile` to `ghcr.io/knt048/vedette-<service>:<version>`; the digest is read back with `podman manifest inspect <repo>@<digest>`, which refuses bytes that do not hash to it (measured with podman 5.7 against a fake registry: "Manifest does not match provided manifest digest"), and the platform set must be exactly PLATFORMS on the local list, the pushed list and the version tag. The tag is for people; nothing downstream reads a tag. Refused: any registry but `ghcr.io/knt048` except a loopback rehearsal (127.0.0.1, [::1], localhost; Linux only; only there TLS verification and the release guards are off; superseded by D-460: only TLS verification and the git checks are off, the `-test.` refusal stays and a rehearsal needs a `gates.json` like a release), a `-test.` version, a dirty tracked tree, HEAD other than kien's tag `v<version>`, `CONTAINER=docker` (the OCI-archive path would need skopeo/regctl, a new dependency). `images.json` (fixed schema: version, images[service, repo, index_digest, platforms[platform, digest]]) is written only after all four are read back; part C reads it for `cosign attest`. (2) **`release-in`** writes `release.in.json` from `images.json` (strict; a rehearsal's file is refused) and the two SemVer-named `.deb`: index digests, platforms, `size` = largest unpacked platform size of the local list (free-space check only, D-104), `install_modes` appliance+container (D-451), `released_at` empty; `channel` and `rollback.safe` must be given, never defaulted; an existing file is never overwritten. (3) **`release-publish`** re-runs the box's verifier, records each file's SHA-256 and size, verifies again and compares (so the record is of verified bytes; symlinks refused), refuses a `-test.` version, verifies `install.sh` and records the very bytes it verified (signed by the manifest's key, trusted comment `file:install.sh version:<v>`; every line that can set one of the three baked variables, in any shell form, must be exactly the baked line equal to the signed manifest's version and package hashes; a manifest without both packages is refused), checks each `.deb` against the signed manifest, requires the tag; with `PUBLISH=1` the signers must be the production keys compiled into the build, compared as whole public keys (key ids are 8 bytes anyone can copy) and every cosign key verify used must be a compiled-in one (backup key only for a rescue; `-keys-dir` never admits another signer), and the live `index.json` + `.minisig` of the `index` release are downloaded and verified: byte-identical to this run's own index → an earlier run uploaded it, only the assets are checked; otherwise they must equal `RELEASE_PREV_INDEX` byte for byte (mandatory; only `-first-release` with no live index skips it). A rescue whose live index the leaked key's holder replaced (D-259) is therefore refused by the tool and published by hand with the printed commands (plan §2); so is the repair of an index left half replaced by an interrupted upload. Then: `gh release create v<v> --verify-tag --draft --notes-file`, re-hash and upload all assets, read back name/size/`sha256` (no digest from GitHub → download and hash) and no extra asset (named with `gh release delete-asset`), anonymous pull of every image digest (`GET https://ghcr.io/token?scope=repository:knt048/vedette-<svc>:pull`, `HEAD /v2/…/manifests/<digest>` with the OCI index and Docker list Accept types; denied → "make the package public", the release stays a draft), `gh release edit --draft=false`, then **last**, after the pull check and the live index are checked again, `index.json` + `.minisig` to the release `index` with `--clobber`, read back. A re-run fills a draft again, compares a published version and never changes it (a bad release is followed by the next version and a `release` revocation). (4) **kien by hand**: tags (AI creates no tag), the one-time `index` release, the ghcr and gh tokens, making the four ghcr packages public after the first push, and keeping GitHub immutable releases off (they would lock the weekly-replaced `index` release). | Draft → attach → publish is what GitHub prescribes for releases whose assets must not change after publication ("immutable releases … assets and associated Git tag cannot be changed after publication"; recommended flow: create a draft, attach all assets, then publish: https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/supply-chain-security/understanding-your-software-supply-chain/immutable-releases, read 2026-11-12) and what `gh release create` does itself when given assets (`gh release create --help`, gh 2.103.3). Sigstore: "you should always sign images based on their digest (`@sha256:...`) rather than a tag … otherwise you might sign something you didn't intend to" (https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/README.md, read 2026-11-12), so everything after the push uses the digest the registry returned. `podman manifest push --digestfile` "write[s] the digest of the resulting image to the file", `--all` defaults to true (https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-manifest-push.1.html). The anonymous pull check is the registry token flow of the OCI distribution API that a box's podman uses. Top-tier practice measured on 2026-11-12: Rancher's GitHub release v2.15.3 carries `rancher-images-digests-linux.txt` and `images-digests-sha256sum.txt` beside the images (`gh release view --repo rancher/rancher`), i.e. the digest list is a release artifact as `images.json` is here; Home Assistant publishes `ghcr.io/home-assistant/home-assistant:<version>` as one OCI index with amd64 and arm64 (`podman manifest inspect`), as ghcr + one index per version does here; Grafana ships its `.deb` packages per architecture as release assets (v13.3.1). Not chosen: building with `buildx --push` at release time (pushes something other than what B scanned); a mutable `latest`/`stable` image tag (the box pulls by digest only, D-104); the `index` in the repository or GitHub Pages (D-341 fixed the release-asset URL; Pages adds a second publishing path); deleting and re-creating a published release on failure (customers may already hold its URLs); trusting `-keys-dir` for a real publish (a wrong directory would publish documents no box accepts). Limits: `--clobber` of the index is two uploads, not atomic (a box that reads the new file with the old signature fails closed and retries, D-104, D-341); the git check proves the tree, not that the images were built from it (the version label and B's gates tie them); the rehearsal registry needs Linux (podman machine on macOS has its own 127.0.0.1). | 2026-11-12 |
| D-458 | **Every Vedette container runs under Vedette's own AppArmor profile `vedette-container`, a copy of Podman's `containers-default` whose signal and ptrace rules also match the stacked label crun gives a container under `NoNewPrivileges` (host, S-CORE-7; units of core, sensor, scan, honeypot; follows D-105, D-316 (10), #599).** (1) **What broke** (lab, fresh Ubuntu 24.04.5, kernel 6.8, Podman 4.9.3, profile `containers-default-0.57.4-apparmor1`, rootful Quadlet units with `NoNewPrivileges=true`): every process of `vedette-scan` and `vedette-honeypot` carried the label `containers-default-0.57.4-apparmor1//&crun (mixed)`, and the kernel denied `operation="signal"` from `containers-default-0.57.4-apparmor1` to the peer `containers-default-0.57.4-apparmor1//&crun`: podman-init (`RunInit=true`) could not forward SIGTERM to the worker, so `systemctl stop vedette-scan` took 10 s, ended in SIGKILL (status 137) and left the unit failed; init.py's SIGTERM to its children got EACCES (#599 made init exit anyway); and the SIGURG of Go's goroutine preemption was denied in core (`vedette`), the sensor and nuclei. (2) **Root cause, three parts.** (a) AppArmor 4.0 (Ubuntu 24.04, also 26.04 and Debian 13's `apparmor` package) ships `/etc/apparmor.d/crun`, `profile crun /usr/bin/crun flags=(unconfined) { userns, }`, so crun is no longer "unconfined" but a named profile. (b) crun, when the OCI spec has `noNewPrivileges` and crun itself is confined, writes `stack <profile>` instead of `exec <profile>` ("if confined only way for apparmor to allow change of profile with NNP is with stacking", `set_apparmor_profile` in crun 1.14.1 and main): under no_new_privs the kernel allows leaving a named profile only as a stack. The container's label becomes the stack of both. (c) The kernel keeps a stack sorted by profile name and matches a peer rule first against the whole label (`A//&B`), then against each part with the permissions intersected (`aa_label_match`, `label_compound_match`, `label_components_match` in `security/apparmor/label.c`). `containers-default` allows `signal (send,receive) peer=<its own name>` only; the whole label does not match that, and the part `crun` has only `signal (receive) peer=…crun*` there, no `send`: every signal between two processes of a container, and to a thread of the same process, is refused. Upstream fixed the template on 2026-11-06 (`signal (send,receive) peer={{.Name}}//&*` and the same for ptrace, container-libs PR 919, commit 6506a4c7f388) for the same stack seen on Ubuntu 25.10+/26.04 and CRI-O; it is in no release yet (backports to Podman 5.8/6.2 "might take a few more weeks"), so Ubuntu 24.04 (Podman 4.9.3, common 0.57.4+ds1-2ubuntu0.2), Ubuntu 26.04 (Podman 5.7.0, common 0.66.0; this machine's `/usr/bin/podman` carries only `peer={{.Name}}`) and Debian 13 (Podman 5.4.2; its `apparmor` package ships `/etc/apparmor.d/crun` too) all have the bug, and no noble SRU is filed. Ubuntu 26.04 kernels from 7.0.0-41 also force a `//&unconfined` stack on exec'd processes even without no_new_privs (Launchpad #2172640, containerd #12886 on 6.17), so the stacked peer is not only a crun/NNP matter. (3) **What ships**: `deploy/deb/vedette-container.apparmor`, installed by the `vedette-host` .deb as `/etc/apparmor.d/vedette-container` (a conffile, as Debian ships every profile; apt runs with `--force-confold`): Podman's template at 6506a4c7f388 with a fixed name, the parser-version checks dropped (every supported parser is ≥ 2.8.96), and the peer of its own rules written `{,**//&}vedette-container{,//&**}` for `signal (send,receive)` and `ptrace (trace,read)`, i.e. this profile alone or stacked with anything in any position (upstream's `{{.Name}}//&*` works for `containers-default` only because "co" sorts before "crun" and "unconfined"; "vedette-container" sorts after them, so its stack is `crun//&vedette-container`). Every other rule (network, capability, file, umount, the /proc and /sys denials, `deny mount`, the receive rules for unconfined, runc, crun, podman) is Podman's. A containers.conf module `/usr/lib/vedette/apparmor-containers.conf` (`[containers] apparmor_profile = "vedette-container"`) in the same package, and one `ContainersConfModule=` line in each of the four unit templates (honeypot: before its own module). Legacy templates `core-4`, `sensor-1`, `honeypot-2`, `scan-1` (D-316 (10)): units migrate at the next host start and take effect at the next restart; no host port is added (D-455 does not defer it). The postinst, only where `aa-enabled --quiet` (Debian's dh_apparmor gate; off, or not manageable as in a container: skipped), compiles the profile before it creates anything (`apparmor_parser --skip-kernel-load --skip-cache`), loads it (`--replace --skip-read-cache --write-cache`, dh_apparmor's `-r -T -W`, which also gives running containers the new rules) and checks the effect (`vedette-container (<mode>)`, any mode, in `/sys/kernel/security/apparmor/profiles`); any failure stops the package (a self-update is then reverted, the box keeps working as before). At boot `apparmor.service` (`Before=sysinit.target`) loads it from `/etc/apparmor.d`, the only directory it reads, before any unit. Podman refuses a container whose named profile is not loaded ("specified but not loaded") but ignores a containers.conf `apparmor_profile` where AppArmor is off or `apparmor_parser` is missing (`setupApparmor`, `apparmor.IsEnabled`), which is why the name goes through a module and not `--security-opt` (that one refuses to start without AppArmor). `NoNewPrivileges=true` and `RunInit=true` stay. (4) **Tests**: `deploy/deb` pins the profile's name and every signal/ptrace line, samples Podman's denials, refuses loosening keywords, compiles it with the machine's `apparmor_parser` when present, runs the postinst's real functions with recorders (off, on, compile failure, load failure, kernel list missing), and checks the package files, the one conffile and that module, profile and `ops.AppArmorProfile` agree; `host/ops` golden units, pins and legacy goldens; `modules/host` INV-17 (every unit names the module, honeypot both). The effect (labels, denials gone, a 2 s stop) is a lab line on 24.04, 26.04 and Debian 13 (`.ai/deferred/fix-apparmor-signals-nnp.md`). (5) **A profile that is not in the kernel stops every container, core's too, so (review r1)**: the postinst refuses, before it creates anything, a missing profile file (dpkg never brings back a deleted conffile; the message names `dpkg -i --force-confmiss --force-confdef --force-confold /var/lib/vedette-host/selfupdate/packages/vedette-host_$(/usr/lib/vedette/vedette-host -version)_$(dpkg --print-architecture).deb`, the package install.sh keeps; until D-412 it named `apt-get install --reinstall … vedette-host`, which cannot work: no box has an apt source for vedette-host) and an administrator's disable link `/etc/apparmor.d/disable/vedette-container` (`aa-disable`; loading it anyway would undo their choice, keeping it means no container starts); at every start `vedette-host`, where Podman's own test holds (`/sys/module/apparmor/parameters/enabled` is `Y`, `/sys/kernel/security/apparmor` exists, `apparmor_parser` is in `/usr/sbin` or `/sbin`; otherwise Podman ignores the name and the host says nothing) and the kernel's list lacks `vedette-container (…)`, runs, beside `startHP` and joined before READY with a 20 s bound (so the D-121 start budget does not grow), the one fixed argv `apparmor_parser --replace --skip-read-cache --write-cache /etc/apparmor.d/vedette-container` (not when disabled or the file is gone) and audits `container.start apparmor_profile_loaded` or `apparmor_profile_missing {reason}`, never blocking its start; RUNBOOK §8.5 has the repair. The package now has a conffile, so the applier's `dpkg -i` of a self-update (and of its rollback) carries `--force-confdef --force-confold` like its apt call: without them dpkg stops at the conffile prompt with stdin on `/dev/null`. Purge also removes the compiled cache `/var/cache/apparmor/*/vedette-container` (dh_apparmor's postrm does the same). After `apt remove` without purge the units stay and name the removed module, so the containers do not start until the package is back. | Why: the other ways out. **Drop `NoNewPrivileges`** (crun then uses `exec`, no stack, on 24.04 GA): rejected, it is the one setting that keeps a setuid binary from raising privilege inside the container (the scan image is Debian slim with its setuid tools; `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` is required by the Kubernetes "restricted" Pod Security Standard, https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards/), and it would not help on 26.04 kernels that stack `unconfined` anyway (LP #2172640). **Worker as PID 1 without `RunInit`** (Go reaps): fixes only the scan stop; SIGURG and every other in-container signal stay denied. **Wait for upstream**: the fix is days old and unreleased; Ubuntu 24.04's Podman 4.9.3 would need an SRU nobody filed, so a supported box would keep the 10 s SIGKILL stop and degraded Go preemption for its whole life. **JIM's way** (one line `signal peer=@{profile_name}//&{crun,podman},` in `/etc/apparmor.d/abstractions/base.d/`, https://github.com/TetronIO/JIM/pull/1975): rejected, it changes every profile on the machine that includes `abstractions/base`, the administrator's too, and needs the cached `containers-default` unloaded. **`apparmor=unconfined`** or disabling the `crun` profile: drops confinement or breaks unprivileged user namespaces for every user (and 26.04 stacks regardless). A named, package-shipped profile per workload is how the top-tier platforms do it: Kubernetes `appArmorProfile.type: Localhost` with profiles loaded on the node (https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/security/apparmor/), Docker/Podman `--security-opt apparmor=<name>` with containers.conf `apparmor_profile` as the default name (https://github.com/containers/common/blob/main/docs/containers.conf.5.md), Debian's dh_apparmor for loading at install. Cost: our copy can drift from Podman's later fixes; the header names the upstream commit, and when every supported distribution ships a Podman whose default handles stacks the units can go back to it (deferred line). Go impact without the fix: Go 1.14+ preempts a goroutine with SIGURG via `tgkill`; when that is refused the runtime falls back to cooperative preemption at function calls, so it keeps working, but a loop without calls cannot be stopped for a GC stop-the-world or the scheduler, and every attempt writes an audit line (https://go.dev/doc/go1.14#runtime, https://github.com/golang/go/issues/24543). Sources: Launchpad #2040483 (crun's AppArmor 4.0 profile and the receive rules, Fix Released noble) https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/libpod/+bug/2040483 ; Launchpad #2118824 (NNP with crun's profile, noble, still Confirmed) https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/podman/+bug/2118824 ; Launchpad #2172640 (26.04 kernel 7.0.0-42 forced `//&unconfined`) https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/linux/+bug/2172640 ; container-libs PR 919 https://github.com/podman-container-tools/container-libs/pull/919 and the template https://github.com/podman-container-tools/container-libs/blob/main/common/pkg/apparmor/apparmor_linux_template.go ; CRI-O #10036 https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/issues/10036 ; containerd #12886 https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/12886 and PR #14487 https://github.com/containerd/containerd/pull/14487 ; crun `set_apparmor_profile` https://github.com/containers/crun/blob/1.14.1/src/libcrun/utils.c ; kernel label matching https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v6.8/security/apparmor/label.c ; Podman `setupApparmor` https://github.com/containers/podman/blob/v4.9.3/pkg/specgen/generate/security_linux.go and `CheckProfileAndLoadDefault` https://github.com/containers/common/blob/v0.57.4/pkg/apparmor/apparmor_linux.go ; Quadlet `ContainersConfModule=` (repeatable, 4.8+) https://github.com/containers/podman/blob/v4.9.3/docs/source/markdown/podman-systemd.unit.5.md ; Debian trixie `apparmor` file list (ships `/etc/apparmor.d/crun`) https://packages.debian.org/trixie/amd64/apparmor/filelist . | 2026-11-12 |
| D-459 | **A software update crosses a sensor protocol bump: core switches first, core takes protocol N and N-1 (S-CORE-2, v1 blocker from lab T5).** (1) **Order**: Apply = [helper,] pull every image, **core's switch first** (step `restart`, with the snapshot), then `container.start` of the sensor, scan worker and honeypot (step `start`), sent by the NEW core after it restarted; steps `[host,] download, restart, start`. The host judges a sensor or scan worker healthy only when core takes its heartbeat (`cmd/vedette-sensor/health.go`), so they are judged only once core runs the new release. Before each of those calls the follower reads the host's state: a core that does not run the target (a rollback that put the database back resumed the run from the copy made before core's switch) stops the run there and the rollback is rebuilt from the host's record. Rollback keeps its order, the reverse: the others first (back to a protocol the running core takes), core last. (2) **Skew**: `core/sensorlink` takes `X-Vedette-Proto` = `ProtoVersion` or `ProtoPrevious` (= ProtoVersion − 1, a test keeps it so); a sensor or worker newer than core, or two behind, stays 426. A bump keeps core able to serve the old peer: new request fields optional (proto 3 has no `capture_error` = none); a bump that changes a reply must first pass the request's protocol to the handler and answer the old shape. A release that bumps the protocol to N sets `min_upgrade_from` no lower than the first release with N-1. (3) **A failure after core's switch** no longer rolls anything back (D-342 (3) chose all-or-nothing because skew was untested; it is now supported): core and the services already switched stay on the new release, the failed one went back by itself (or did not move) and keeps working with core; the run is `failed` and says so ("Vedette itself runs X. It keeps working with the services still on Y, which move with the next update. To put the whole box back on Y, use Rollback."), with a history entry (`moved`); the 6-hour rule after core's switch also writes it and says that core runs X and points to Rollback. A failure up to core's switch has changed nothing else (no undo). (4) **Limit**: the plan is made by the release being left, so only updates FROM a release with D-459 use this order; a box on 0.0.1-test.16 still reverts on a protocol bump and is reinstalled with `install.sh` (no release is tagged stable yet). | Kubernetes version skew policy: the control plane is upgraded first and a kubelet must never be newer than kube-apiserver, it may be older (https://kubernetes.io/releases/version-skew-policy/); Elastic: Elasticsearch, Kibana and Fleet Server are upgraded before the Elastic Agents they serve, and an agent may not be newer than Fleet Server (https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elastic-stack/current/upgrading-elastic-stack.html, https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/fleet/current/upgrade-elastic-agent.html). Neither rolls the control plane back when a node or agent upgrade fails: the older node keeps working inside the supported skew and is retried. Not chosen: the sensor falling back to the old protocol on 426 (a newer agent than its server is the case both products refuse, and it would hide a wrong order); rolling core back automatically after a later service fails (core's rollback may put the database back, which needs the administrator's confirmation, D-342 (8)). Lab evidence: T5 upgrade lab (Ubuntu 24.04, 2026-11-13) 0.0.1-test.16 (proto 3) → test.17 (proto 4, #607/D-399): sensor switched first, 426 `proto_unsupported`, health failed, run reverted every time; rollback then 409 `no_previous`. | 2026-11-13 |
| D-460 | **The release gates keep a record, and every later step ships only what it names; a rehearsal is as strict as a release (WP-08k).** (1) The final `release gates` run (`make release-gates`, step 3) writes `dist/release/gates.json` only when every check passed: the version, the floor, per `.deb` arch its file name, SHA-256 and size (the bytes compared with the rebuild), per image and platform the **config digest** (podman's image ID; it equals trivy's `Metadata.ImageID` only for an OCI-format image, so `make images` builds podman images with `--format oci`: a Docker-format build is converted on export and its digest changes), and that digest must also be the image the kept trivy report (`dist/vuln/<local>-<arch>.json`, `Metadata.ImageID`) and SBOM (`dist/sbom/<local>-<arch>.cdx.json`, `aquasecurity:trivy:ImageID`) were made of. `make release-gates` removes an earlier record on its first line, so any failing step leaves none; `-preflight` writes nothing. The config digest is chosen over the local manifest digest because the rest of the chain already uses it (push compares a list already in the registry by it, `images.json` records it, part C requires the SBOM's ImageID to equal it); a re-read of the same list gives the same one, a rebuild another. (2) `release push` (all four lists checked before anything is pushed, and each list read again after its own push), `release in` (each `.deb`, `images.json` and the local lists) and `release manifest` (the `.deb` hashes the manifest names, so bake-install and publish inherit it) read it strictly and refuse a missing record, another version or other bytes: "run make release-gates again". (3) A rehearsal against a loopback registry gets no bypass and no rehearsal record: a real SemVer version tagged locally in a scratch clone, steps 1–3 with `MIN_SEQUENCE=0`, then `release-push REGISTRY=127.0.0.1:<port>`; `-test.` is refused there too. This replaces the rehearsal part of D-457 ("only there TLS verification and the release guards are off": now only TLS verification and the git checks are). | A `make images` or `make host-deb` between step 3 and steps 4–8, or during the scans of step 3, would otherwise ship bytes the gates never saw (Opus review of #614, M; review round 1 of this branch, M1–M3). Leading practice binds every later step to the digest that was checked: SLSA's verification step is "Verify that statement's subject matches the digest of the artifact in question" (https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.2/verifying-artifacts; Build L3 requirements https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/requirements, opened 2026-11-12, v1.0 page marked retired in favour of 1.2); cosign attestations name the image by its sha256 digest in the in-toto subject (https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/verifying/attestation/, opened 2026-11-12); GoReleaser builds once and signs the artifacts and checksums of that same run before uploading them (https://goreleaser.com/customization/sign/, opened 2026-11-12). A rehearsal bypass would be a second path that ships without the gates; the lead chose strict over convenience. Plan: `docs/plans/2026-11-12-wp08k-release-job.md`. | 2026-11-13 |
| D-461 | **The RFC 6598 shared address space 100.64.0.0/10 (carrier-grade NAT inside an ISP or a company network, Tailscale) is a local network for the scan and watch scope, like RFC 1918; the rest of 100.0.0.0/8 stays public; every "is this on the Internet" guard keeps refusing 100.64/10 (S-CORE-1, S-INV-1; kien's N100, setup step "Network to watch", 2026-11-13).** (1) **Before**: the setup wizard refused `100.65.254.0/24` with "is not a private range (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16)" (GUI `isPrivateCidr`, mock, `parseLan`), so a box on a LAN numbered from 100.64/10 could not be set up at all. (2) **One rule, one place**: new leaf package `core/localnet` (standard library only: `net/netip`, `slices`; its own leaf test; the sensor binary links it through `nmapargv` and `nucleiargv`, whose leaf tests and `TestBinaryDependencies`/`TestGoListDepsOfTheSensorBinary` now allow exactly it): `Addr(a)` = plain IPv4 in 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16 or 100.64/10; `Prefix(p)` = an IPv4 range inside one of them and not wider (100.0.0.0/8, 100.64.0.0/9, 10.0.0.0/7 refused); `Names` = "10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x, 100.64-127.x" for the error sentences. Web: one `isPrivateCidr` (`web/src/features/inventory/validate.ts`, now reading the range's network so host bits never change the answer; `features/core/util.ts` re-exports it) and `LOCAL_RANGE_NAMES`. (3) **Changed (scope or local-device meaning)**: setup `parseLan` and the box-network prefill of `GET /core/setup/modules` (a CGNAT management network is offered too; the /16 cap stays, so a whole /10 is never offered); Devices → Scope (`inventory.checkRanges`, GUI `rangeProblem`, mock, hint text); CSV import note (`ipNote`: a 100.64/10 device is "outside your saved ranges", not "a public address"); nmap targets (`nmapargv.validTarget`, both core and worker); nuclei targets (`nucleiargv.validHost`, both sides); logs' LAN device of a connection (`signature.LocalOK`) and response's matching check of `logs.ioc_hit.detected` (`events.go`, now `signature.LocalOK`, so the two modules agree). Error code stays `public_range`; the sentences now end the range list with "100.64-127.x". (4) **Unchanged on purpose (public-internet meaning, SSRF/IOC guards)**: feeds dial and normalize (a feed never lists or reaches 100.64/10), notify webhook and `http` rule, logs SIEM send, `signature.PublicDest` (a 100.64/10 destination is never looked up), response block list and `PortOpened` (exposure), exposure validate/detect (a box behind CGNAT still gets `not_public`), scan surface, ai news fetch, `core/conn`, `core/netguard`, `ai/provider` (already counts 100.64/10 as internal for "inside the network" profiles: same meaning, untouched), `modules/core/updates_check.go` test base, `cmd/vedette/tls.go` (already includes 100.64/10 as global unicast in the certificate). (5) **Limit**: inside an ISP's CGNAT the 100.64/10 neighbours can be other customers' routers; the setup commitment ("these ranges belong to my company and I am allowed to scan them") and the scope confirmation already put that choice on the admin, exactly as for RFC 1918 space in a shared building. The Alibaba Cloud metadata address 100.100.100.200 lies in 100.64/10: nuclei never targets it (`nucleiargv.validHost` refuses it on core and worker, like every other guard that lists it, `core/netguard`), because nuclei keeps up to 4 KB of an answer as evidence that can reach a BYOK AI provider; nmap may still probe it (port states only, no body kept). During an update window (core first), an older worker refuses a whole sweep batch that mixes RFC 1918 and 100.64/10 addresses, so some RFC 1918 hosts wait for the next pass (sensor-protocol §10); no proto bump. | Why: RFC 6598 (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6598 §1, §4) defines 100.64/10 as Shared Address Space that MUST NOT be forwarded across provider boundaries, and IANA marks it "Globally Reachable: False" (https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv4-special-registry/iana-ipv4-special-registry.xhtml); companies and Tailscale number real LANs from it (Tailscale: https://tailscale.com/kb/1015/100.x-addresses, "addresses aren't exposed to the public internet"). Browsers' Private Network Access treats it as private address space (WICG spec §2.1, https://wicg.github.io/private-network-access/#ip-address-space-heading: `100.64.0.0/10` → private). OPNsense's "Block private networks" covers "RFC 1918, loopback, link-local and carrier-grade NAT" (https://docs.opnsense.org/manual/interfaces.html), while pfSense's covers RFC 1918 and loopback only (https://docs.netgate.com/pfsense/en/latest/interfaces/configure.html) and runZero's `private` keyword names "RFC-1918 and private use" (https://help.runzero.com/docs/discovering-assets/): the leading products differ, and the ones that judge "is this a local network" (PNA, OPNsense, Tailscale) side with local. Not chosen: all of 100.0.0.0/8 (most of it is routed public space); a separate opt-in switch (one more setting nobody asked for; the scope confirmation already is the opt-in); widening the public-address guards (a CGNAT address is still never a public egress IP to verify or a feed entry to look up). | 2026-11-13 |
| D-462 | **The first-run setup wizard has three steps (Account, Network, Modules); the Alerts step is gone (kien, 2026-11-13).** Finish setup on Modules creates the box and lands on Home; it and Back are off while finishing, the 2nd/3rd click of a double/triple click (`MouseEvent.detail` > 1) never submits a step (a time window after entering a step was not chosen: it would also drop a fast but deliberate click, as automation makes), and ranges the box refuses send the admin back to Network. Alert channels are set up later only in Settings → Alert channels; Home shows an administrator "No alert channel yet" with a **Set up an alert channel** link there while no channel is saved and switched on (read from the existing `GET /notify/channels`, only when the Notifications module is on), and the reminder goes once one is. No snooze: an admin who wants no alerts switches Notifications off and the reminder says so. API unchanged: `POST /core/setup` never carried a channel (the wizard called `PUT /notify/channels/{type}` itself); the GUI helper `saveNotifyChannel` and the wizard-only `ChannelType` are removed.
